lessons.title: Measuring resource performance
lessons.html:
What optimising means

Optimising resources means getting the most saleable fish from the water, feed, energy, labour, equipment and money available, without harming fish welfare or the environment. It starts with measurement: you cannot improve what you do not measure.

Key performance indicators (KPIs)

ResourceKPI
FeedFeed conversion ratio (FCR), feed cost per kg produced
StockSurvival %, growth rate, harvest weight uniformity
Waterm3 used per kg produced
EnergykWh and diesel litres per kg produced
LabourLabour hours and cost per tonne
FacilitiesKg produced per m3 of tank or per hectare of pond per year
MoneyProduction cost per kg vs selling price

Gathering the data

Use existing records: feeding sheets, sample weighings, mortality logs, electricity and fuel accounts, timesheets and harvest records. Calculate KPIs per batch and per unit, and compare units, batches, seasons and suppliers. The best units show what is achievable; the worst show where to look.

Finding the causes

When a KPI is poor, ask why several times. For example: FCR is high. Why? Feed is left over. Why? Fish eat less on cold mornings but the ration was not reduced. Why? The feeding chart is not adjusted for temperature. Action: introduce a temperature-adjusted feeding table and train feeders. This root-cause approach avoids treating symptoms only.

Prioritising

Focus first on the largest costs and biggest losses. On most farms that means feed efficiency and survival, followed by energy. A one-point improvement in survival or a small drop in FCR is often worth more than cutting minor costs.

lessons.title: Implementing improvements
lessons.html:
Practical optimisation measures

Feed

  • Feed to appetite and adjust rations to temperature and fish size.
  • Match pellet size to fish size as they grow.
  • Improve storage to stop spoilage and rodent losses.
  • Use demand or timed feeders where they reduce waste, and check them daily.

Stock and facilities

  • Grade regularly for uniform growth.
  • Stock to the density each unit can carry with its water flow and aeration, not more.
  • Reduce turnaround time between harvest and restocking so units are not idle.
  • Improve biosecurity to raise survival.

Water and energy

  • Fix leaks and maintain valves.
  • Run aerators according to measured oxygen demand, for example more at night and in hot weather, while never compromising safety margins.
  • Use efficient pumps and motors when replacing equipment; consider solar for daytime pumping.
  • Reuse water through recirculation, aquaponics or irrigation where it is suitable and permitted.

Labour

  • Plan work so routine tasks are done in set sequences with less walking and waiting.
  • Train staff to cover several tasks; use a skills matrix.

Implementing change well

  1. Agree the change and the expected result with the manager.
  2. Trial it on one or two units first, with a control unit for comparison.
  3. Measure the result over a fair period.
  4. Roll out if it works; update procedures and train staff.
  5. Keep monitoring so gains are not lost.

Cost-benefit thinking

Before investing, compare cost with expected saving. Example: a more efficient aerator costs R20 000 and saves R800 of electricity a month; it pays back in 25 months. The figures are illustrative; use real quotes and meter readings.

Never optimise by cutting safety: backup aeration, protective equipment and safe staffing levels are not negotiable.

Key points

  • Measure KPIs per kg produced for feed, water, energy, labour and money.
  • Find root causes before acting.
  • Focus first on feed efficiency and survival.
  • Trial changes on a few units, measure, then roll out.
  • Use simple payback calculations before investing.
